result: FUN025 mice were isolated from an ENU mutagenesis project and exhibit retinal abnormalities similar to aged WT mice. Age-dependent abnormalities in WT retina start from the peripheral retina and progress centrally, with timing dependent on genetic background (A/J vs B6).
evaluation: Claims C1-C5 are all supported by citations to prior work (Pinto et al., 2004; Vitaterna et al., 2006; Higuchi et al., 2015). These claims establish the background context for the study and are appropriately attributed to previous publications.

result: FUN025 mice show early-onset and progressive retinal aging phenotypes including decreased ONLT index (photoreceptor loss), ectopic synapses, and increased GFAP (retinal stress), all progressing from peripheral to central retina by 2-7 months of age.
evaluation: Claims C6-C17 are well-supported by histological and immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1A-E. The quantification shows statistically significant differences (p<0.05) between FUN025 and WT mice at multiple time points and retinal locations. The spatial and temporal progression pattern is clearly demonstrated.

result: FUN025 mice exhibit punctate light deposits in fundus photography, autofluorescent cells/aggregates between photoreceptors and RPE that resemble lipofuscin and subretinal drusenoid deposits (SDD) observed in AMD patients.
evaluation: Claims C18-C26 are supported by fundus photography (Figure 2A) and microscopy data (Figure 2B). The comparison to lipofuscin and SDD is appropriately qualified as resemblance based on autofluorescence properties and supported by citations. The speculation in C19 is appropriately hedged with 'may be due to'.

result: Subretinal autofluorescent cells in FUN025 mice are positive for microglia (Iba1) and macrophage (F4/80) markers, with morphological features suggesting transformation from microglia to macrophages and migration toward the RPE as the origin of stress.
evaluation: Claims C27-C31 are supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2C and citations to prior work on microglial behavior. The inference about transformation (C30) and RPE as stress origin (C31) are reasonable interpretations of the morphological and marker data, though these remain inferential rather than directly demonstrated.

result: FUN025 mice show increased immunoreactivity to inflammasome markers (NLRP3 and caspase-1 p10) in neural retina and RPE, indicating elevated innate immunity consistent with aging and age-dependent diseases.
evaluation: Claims C32-C36 are supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2D and appropriate citations. The general knowledge claims about innate immunity (C32-C33) are properly cited. The interpretation that increased markers indicate elevated innate immunity (C36) is reasonable and supported by citation.

result: By seven months, FUN025 mice show uniformly thickened RPE with intact individual cells, similar to observations in AMD patients regarding innate immunity markers and RPE thickness.
evaluation: Claims C37-C40 are supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2E showing RPE thickness with intact nuclei. The comparison to AMD patients (C39-C40) is appropriately supported by citations. Statistical significance is shown in Figure 2E.

result: ERG recordings show significantly reduced scotopic a-wave and b-wave (rod pathway) and modest reduction in photopic b-wave (cone pathway) in FUN025 mice, indicating impaired visual function and establishing FUN025 as a model of accelerated retinal aging and age-dependent disease.
evaluation: Claims C41-C44 are supported by ERG data in Figure 2F showing statistically significant differences (two-way ANOVA). The functional impairment conclusion (C43) is a reasonable inference from the ERG data. The overall conclusion (C44) is well-supported by the cumulative evidence from C6-C43.

result: Genetic mapping identified a point mutation (T>C) in the splice-donor site adjacent to exon 12 of Tmem135, which disrupts the splice site resulting in exon 12 skipping and a frameshift creating an early stop codon.
evaluation: Claims C45-C52 are well-supported by genetic mapping data (Figure 3A), sequencing data (Figure 3B-D,F), and appropriate citation for splice site consensus sequences (C49). The molecular characterization is thorough and the conclusions about the mutation's effects are directly demonstrated.

result: The FUN025 mutation results in predicted loss of the 4th and 5th transmembrane helices, reversed orientation of remaining helices, and shorter c-terminal region, likely impairing normal TMEM135 protein function.
evaluation: Claims C53-C57 are supported by computational predictions using TMHMM software (Figure 3G and supplement). However, these are predictions rather than experimental determinations of protein structure. The conclusion that function is likely impaired (C57) is reasonable but remains inferential. The predictions should ideally be validated experimentally.

result: Western blot detected both mutant and WT TMEM135 protein. Complementation testing with CRISPR-generated T>C mice showed non-complementation, confirming the T>C mutation in Tmem135 as the FUN025 causative mutation.
evaluation: Claims C58-C64 are well-supported by western blot data (Figure 3H) and complementation test data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). The complementation test is a rigorous genetic approach that definitively establishes causality. The phenotypic similarity in compound heterozygotes strongly supports the conclusion.

result: TMEM135 was previously suggested to be involved in fat storage and longevity regulation in C. elegans, but its function is not yet clearly characterized.
evaluation: Claims C65-C66 are appropriately cited to prior work and accurately represent the state of knowledge about TMEM135 function at the time of the study. This provides important context for the novelty of the current findings.

result: TMEM135 localizes to mitochondria in multiple cell types and tissues, showing punctate distribution along mitochondrial surface, at constriction sites, and at tips. Colocalization is reduced in FUN025 cells. A proportion of TMEM135 is strongly associated with mitochondria in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C67-C82 are extensively supported by multiple complementary approaches: immunofluorescence (Figure 4A,B,D,E,G,H), immunoelectron microscopy (Figure 4C), and biochemical fractionation (Figure 4F). The localization is demonstrated across multiple cell types and in vivo. The reduced colocalization in FUN025 cells (C72, C81) is shown but not quantified statistically. The speculation about other organelles (C83) is appropriately hedged.

result: Tmem135FUN025/FUN025 cells show over-fused mitochondrial networks with increased size and decreased number, while Tg-Tmem135 cells show over-fragmented networks with decreased size. This indicates TMEM135 regulates the balance between mitochondrial fission and fusion.
evaluation: Claims C84-C97 are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence: microscopy (Figure 5A), morphology scoring (Figure 5B), quantitative measurements (Figure 5C-E), siRNA knockdown (Figure 5F), and electron microscopy of retina (Figure 5G-H). Statistical significance is shown throughout. The conclusion about TMEM135's role in mitochondrial dynamics (C97) is strongly supported by the bidirectional effects of loss-of-function and overexpression.

result: Overexpression of Tmem135 does not inhibit MFN2-induced mitochondrial fusion, and fusion protein levels (OPA1, MFN1, MFN2) are unchanged or decreased in mutant cells, indicating the mitochondrial phenotype is not due to altered fusion protein expression and suggesting TMEM135 does not inhibit fusion.
evaluation: Claims C98-C103 are supported by overexpression experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) and western blots (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B-E). The logic is sound: if TMEM135 inhibited fusion, overexpression should reduce MFN2-induced fusion, which was not observed. The western blot data rule out indirect effects through fusion protein regulation.

result: Some TMEM135 puncta colocalize with DRP1 on mitochondria. DRP1 translocation and assembly into higher-order structures occurs normally in Tmem135FUN025/FUN025 cells, but mitochondria remain fused, suggesting DRP1 stays inactive and TMEM135 may be required for DRP1 activation.
evaluation: Claims C104-C110 are supported by colocalization data (Figure 5—figure supplement 3) and quantification of DRP1 puncta density and intensity (Figure 5J-K). The interpretation that DRP1 is inactive despite normal translocation (C109) is a reasonable inference from the data. The speculation about TMEM135 requirement for DRP1 activation (C110) is appropriately hedged and logically follows from the evidence.

result: Live imaging shows TMEM135 localizes at mitochondrial constriction sites where mitochondria later divide, supporting the conclusion that TMEM135 is involved in mitochondrial fission rather than fusion.
evaluation: Claims C111-C112 are supported by live imaging data (Figure 5L and Videos 1-2). This direct observation of TMEM135 at fission sites provides strong evidence for its role in fission. The conclusion (C112) is well-supported by the cumulative evidence from C98-C111.

result: Tg-Tmem135 cells show increased mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨM) while Tmem135FUN025/FUN025 cells retain similar ΔΨM to WT, indicating individual mitochondrial membrane units remain functional despite altered dynamics.
evaluation: Claims C113-C116 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 6A and supplement 1). The interpretation that membrane units are functional (C116) is reasonable. However, the increased ΔΨM in Tg-Tmem135 cells is somewhat unexpected and could reflect altered mitochondrial physiology beyond just dynamics.

result: Both Tmem135FUN025/FUN025 and Tg-Tmem135 cells show decreased basal OCR and ATP production. Tmem135FUN025/FUN025 cells additionally show decreased maximal respiration and spare respiratory capacity (SRC), while proton leak is unchanged. These differences may be due to altered mitochondrial dynamics.
evaluation: Claims C117-C122 are well-supported by Seahorse respirometry data (Figure 6B-G) with appropriate statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA). The functional consequences of altered mitochondrial dynamics are clearly demonstrated. The speculation that differences are due to dynamics changes (C122) is reasonable but remains inferential as causality is not directly tested.

result: Tmem135FUN025/FUN025 cells have significantly reduced spare respiratory capacity (SRC), suggesting mutant TMEM135 affects both normal oxidative phosphorylation and the ability to produce more energy under stress.
evaluation: Claims C123-C125 are supported by the Seahorse data (Figure 6F) and appropriate citation defining SRC (C123). The interpretation (C125) is reasonable and has important implications for cellular stress responses. The connection to aging is appropriately discussed.

result: Both Tmem135FUN025/FUN025 and Tg-Tmem135 cells show increased total ROS and superoxide. Antioxidant enzymes (SOD1, SOD2, SOD3, GPx1, CAT) are upregulated in Tmem135FUN025/FUN025 cells under normal conditions but cannot be further upregulated by exogenous H2O2, suggesting maximal capacity has been reached.
evaluation: Claims C126-C132 are supported by flow cytometry (Figure 6H-I and supplement 2) and western blots (Figure 6J). The interpretation about maximal antioxidant capacity (C132) is reasonable but somewhat speculative. Alternative explanations (e.g., impaired stress response signaling) are not fully excluded. The H2O2 treatment conditions and timing should be better justified.

result: Under hyperoxic conditions (75% O2), Tmem135FUN025/FUN025 retinas show greater susceptibility to oxidative stress-induced cell death (ONLT index, TUNEL), increased GFAP, and upregulation of lipid peroxidation marker 4-HNE. TMEM135 protein levels increase in mutant retina under both normal and hyperoxic conditions, suggesting a protective role against oxidative stress.
evaluation: Claims C133-C140 are supported by in vivo hyperoxia experiments with histology (Figure 7A), TUNEL assay (Figure 7B), immunostaining (Figure 7C), and western blots (Figure 7D). Statistical analysis is appropriate (two-way ANOVA). The conclusion about TMEM135's protective role (C140) is well-supported by the differential sensitivity to oxidative stress. Sample sizes are adequate (n=3-4 per group).

result: TMEM135 plays a critical role in maintaining retinal health by regulating mitochondrial dynamics balance. Defects result in accelerated retinal aging and age-dependent disease pathologies. TMEM135 may promote DRP1-dependent fission through DRP1 activation and could be a therapeutic target.
evaluation: Claims C141-C144 represent the main conclusions of the study and are well-supported by the cumulative evidence from all prior results. The mechanistic proposal about DRP1 activation (C143) is appropriately hedged as speculative. The therapeutic potential (C144) is reasonable speculation based on the findings but would require extensive additional work to validate.

result: Background on aging and age-dependent diseases: oxidative stress damage accumulates with age, ROS are generated mainly in mitochondria, mitochondrial dysfunction occurs in aging and age-dependent diseases, but molecular mechanisms linking aging and disease are not well understood.
evaluation: Claims C145-C156 provide background context and are appropriately supported by citations to established literature. These are general knowledge claims that set up the rationale for the study. The citations appear appropriate for the claims made.

result: The FUN025 phenotypes suggest the responsible gene regulates retinal aging rate and its impairment leads to age-dependent disease. The retinal aging process is accelerated in Tmem135FUN025/FUN025 mice. A single gene mutation leads to both accelerated aging and disease pathologies, supporting the idea that accelerating aging may lead to age-dependent diseases.
evaluation: Claims C157-C161 represent interpretations and conclusions drawn from the phenotypic characterization. These are well-supported by the data presented in the Results section. The connection between accelerated aging and disease (C161) is appropriately presented as a supported hypothesis rather than proven fact.

result: Similar pathologies (drusen, ectopic synapses, photoreceptor degeneration) are observed in AMD patients with earlier onset/increased severity. TMEM135 may be a key molecule that tips normal aging toward age-dependent diseases.
evaluation: Claim C162 is appropriately supported by citations to AMD literature. Claim C163 is speculative but reasonable based on the study's findings. The speculation is appropriately hedged with 'may be'.

result: The RPE may be the primary site affected by the Tmem135FUN025 mutation, as evidenced by microglial migration patterns, morphological changes, and earlier RPE abnormalities than photoreceptor degeneration. This is consistent with current AMD pathogenesis hypotheses.
evaluation: Claims C164-C173 present a well-reasoned interpretation of the data regarding RPE as the primary affected site. The evidence from microglial morphology and migration (C167) is supported by Figure 2C. The timing of RPE vs photoreceptor abnormalities (C169) is supported by the data. The comparison to AMD pathogenesis (C172) is appropriately cited. The overall conclusion (C173) is a reasonable inference.

result: Background on ROS and mitochondrial dysfunction: dysfunctional mitochondria generate more ROS leading to oxidative damage. Superoxide is the principal ROS from the electron transport chain. Oxidative stress can induce mitochondrial fragmentation.
evaluation: Claims C174-C176 provide relevant background information. C174 and C175 are general knowledge appropriately stated. C176 is supported by citations and provides context for interpreting the Tg-Tmem135 phenotype.

result: Background on spare respiratory capacity (SRC): SRC exhaustion is associated with various diseases, and mitochondria may contribute to aging through life-long SRC decrease.
evaluation: Claims C177-C178 provide important context for interpreting the SRC findings and are appropriately supported by citations. This background helps establish the significance of the SRC reduction observed in Tmem135FUN025/FUN025 cells.

result: WT mice can tolerate oxidative stress while Tmem135FUN025/FUN025 mice with declined mitochondrial function have lower tolerance. Mutant mice are more susceptible to environmental stressors, leading to accelerated aging and early-onset age-dependent diseases.
evaluation: Claims C179-C181 are well-supported by the hyperoxia experiments (Figure 7) and the cumulative evidence of mitochondrial dysfunction. The interpretation logically connects the cellular phenotypes to the in vivo aging phenotypes.

result: TMEM135 is critical for regulating aging process onset and progression, and defects lead to age-dependent diseases. TMEM135 presents a novel molecular link between aging and age-dependent diseases.
evaluation: Claims C182-C184 represent the overarching conclusions of the study. These are well-supported by the comprehensive characterization of the FUN025 phenotype, identification of the causative mutation, and mechanistic studies of TMEM135 function. The claim of novelty (C184) is justified given the forward genetics approach and the previously uncharacterized role of TMEM135 in this context.
